name: Hints, Not Answers
title: Hints, Not Answers
answer: Hints, Not Answers is the practice of configuring AI math tools to guide students with one hint at a time instead of solving problems for them. It matters because a high school trial found that students using a plain chatbot scored much higher on practice but 17 percent lower on a later exam taken without AI, while students using a hints-only tutor did not suffer that loss.

sections.body: Most general AI tools will solve a math problem the moment a student asks, which turns practice into something the tool does rather than the student. To make these tools act as tutors, a school sets them up with standing instructions that change how they respond. The tool is told to ask what the student has already tried, to give one hint at a time, and never to show a full solution. This solves the problem of AI quietly replacing the thinking that practice is meant to build, while still giving students help when they are stuck.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, a teacher with a school account in a tool such as Gemini for Education can give the tool standing instructions so it behaves like a tutor rather than an answer machine. The best setups also give the tool the correct answer for each problem, so it does not invent a wrong one while guiding the student. Teachers add common mistakes along with a matching hint for each one. That preparation takes time, but it can be reused every year the unit is taught. The text describes this approach for mathematics from kindergarten through twelfth grade, with its strongest example drawn from a high school trial.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this the strongest evidence in the chapter, and it comes from a warning. In a high school math trial, students using a plain chatbot during practice scored much higher on practice problems but 17 percent lower on a later exam taken without AI (Bastani et al., 2025). Students using a tutor set up to give hints rather than answers did not suffer that loss. The difference came down to how the tool was configured. In that trial, the tutor version was given each problem's solution so it would not invent a wrong one while guiding the student (Bastani et al., 2025).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits here are about configuration and preparation, not about the tool alone. A general AI tool left as it is will solve the problem as soon as a student asks, so the school has to set the standing instructions that make it a tutor. Someone has to supply the correct answer for each problem and pair common mistakes with matching hints, which takes time even though the work can be reused in later years. The decisions about what the tool is told to do, and what counts as a hint rather than a solution, stay with the teacher.
